attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Not happening this decade' is firm, so it is a forecast. The 'maybe not even next' extension is hedged, and the draft correctly keeps it as a qualifier rather than a scored commitment.

contract.note: It reads the deadline as the end of 2029 and treats it as a privately owned personal car earning driverless fares. That is the ordinary reading. Requiring real operation, not announcements, is fair.

evidence.note: Tesla's Oct 21, 2026 earnings call, before the evaluation date. Tesla says customer cars may join the Robotaxi fleet around Q2 2027. That is a company plan, not an operating service.
Lyft's 2025 announcement aims to launch personal Tensor cars on its network in 2027. That is a planned launch, so it neither falsifies nor confirms the forecast.

reviews.rationale: The firm deadline is Dec 31, 2029, which is after the Oct 28, 2026 evaluation date. The packet has no record of a personal car completing paid driverless taxi rides, so the early contradiction rule has not been met. The Tesla and Lyft items are only plans for 2027. Not seeing the event before the deadline does not support the forecast either, so it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post. He draws on press reporting but states the claim as his own view.

semantics.note: This describes Cruise's state at the time of the post: staffing exceeded vehicles and the company was losing money. 'For now' is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'burning money' as consuming funds or running at a loss is fair and ordinary. Requiring a basis 'identified' by the claim would make the claim impossible to score, since no basis was given. I therefore score it on the stated ordinary reading.

evidence.note: Nov 2023 reporting of about 1.5 workers per Cruise vehicle. The CEO did not dispute the figure, called Cruise 'intentionally over staffed', and said the count included fleet-support staff. That matches the contract's definition of support staff. There are no matched primary counts.
GM's Q3 2023 release shows a $732M EBIT-adjusted loss for Cruise. Under the plain reading, that is a large operating loss in the target quarter.

reviews.rationale: Staffing: independent reporting of 1.5 support workers per vehicle went undisputed by the CEO, who called Cruise overstaffed. Money: Cruise lost $732M in Q3 2023 on GM's segment basis. Under the plain reading of operating at a loss, both parts hold. Limits: there are no matched primary headcount and fleet counts, and nothing shows whether remote assistance saved money compared with drivers.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The draft keeps 'essentially', 'comparisons we have heard' and 'in the car or remotely'.

contract.note: Treating 'we have heard' as the public comparisons available before the post, and counting remote guidance as a human role, are reasonable readings. Whether simulated studies count is not settled and could change the result.

evidence.note: A 2020 Waymo paper discloses a remote-assistance team. This shows that riding with no onboard driver does not mean no human was involved.
The Sept 2023 Swiss Re comparison covers rides with no driver on board but does not exclude remote assistance. It fits the claim, but it is only one comparison.
A 2021 simulated replay of fatal crashes is a possible exception if simulations count. It is not a road dataset that excludes remote assistance.

reviews.rationale: The support condition requires a reasonably complete review of comparisons published before the post, and the packet has none. The items examined fit the claim (Swiss Re does not exclude remote help), and the simulated study is a possible exception. Without a count of the full set of comparisons, 'essentially none' cannot be confirmed or refuted.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: 'Will still need human drivers' is a firm forecast. 'Can stop worrying' is advice that rests on it. 'Quite some time' sets no deadline.

contract.note: Scoring the checkable part, continued reliance on human drivers, is fair. Because no deadline was given, the claim can be settled only by a conclusive event.

evidence.note: Uber, May 2026: AVs run only in parts of a few cities and drivers remain central. This fits the forecast, but it is a company statement and not an endpoint.
Lyft, May 2026: a hybrid network that relies on human drivers. This fits the forecast, but it is a company statement about its own strategy.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. Neither Uber nor Lyft has dropped human drivers, so there is no conclusive event. The 2026 company disclosures show continued reliance on drivers, which fits the forecast, but an open-ended forecast cannot be scored as supported before its period can be identified.
